why: Slide a window one step: s[i..j-1] and s[i+1..j] hold the same letters exactly when s[i] == s[j], since one drops s[i] and the other drops s[j]. So for each letter, its first and last occurrence give a pair of length last - first. The two are unequal unless everything between is that same letter. A longer pair is never possible.
hints: Look at two windows of the same length that are shifted by one position. When do they hold the same multiset of letters?

Windows [i, j-1] and [i+1, j] are anagrams exactly when s[i] == s[j]. Pick, for each letter, its first and last positions to get length last - first. They are equal strings only if s[i..j] is one repeated letter.
One pass records first index, last index, and the number of separate runs of each letter. The answer is the max of last - first over letters with at least 2 runs, else -1. O(n).
pitfalls: "aabbcc": each letter forms one run, so every shifted pair is identical: return -1.
A letter appearing in two separate runs (like 'b' in "abcacb") gives last - first, here 5 - 1 = 4.
The two substrings are allowed to overlap.
